package.intro: Benito Mussolini founded the fascist movement in 1919 and ruled Italy as dictator from 1922 to 1943. He crushed opposition at home, waged brutal colonial wars in Libya and Ethiopia, passed racial laws against Italy's Jews, and took his country into a disastrous war as Hitler's ally. This documentary tells how he took power, and how it ended.
facts: Expelled from the Italian Socialist Party in 1914 for supporting entry into the First World War
Founded the Fasci di Combattimento in Milan on 23 March 1919
Appointed prime minister by King Victor Emmanuel III after the March on Rome, October 1922
Socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti was kidnapped and murdered by fascists on 10 June 1924
Italy invaded Ethiopia on 3 October 1935 and used poison gas
Racial laws against Italy's Jews were passed in 1938
Deposed and arrested on 25 July 1943; shot by partisans on 28 April 1945
package.sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, R. J. B. Bosworth's Mussolini, Denis Mack Smith's Mussolini, Christopher Duggan's Fascist Voices, Ian Campbell's The Addis Ababa Massacre, the Fondazione CDEC (Centre for Contemporary Jewish Documentation, Milan).

sections.name: Cold open
lines: On the night of the twenty-fourth of July 1943, in a grand hall in Rome, the leaders of Italy's Fascist Party did something unthinkable. They voted against their own leader.
The next afternoon, Benito Mussolini went to see the king. He was told he had been replaced, and was led out to a waiting ambulance, under arrest.
He had ruled Italy for almost twenty-one years. He invented fascism, the movement that inspired Hitler and gave its name to a whole family of dictatorships.

lines.label: estimated Italian deaths in the Second World War

lines: He waged brutal colonial wars in Africa, passed laws against Italy's Jews, and led his country into a war that killed nearly half a million Italians.
This is the story of the man who invented fascism, how he took power, and how it ended.

sections.name: The young socialist
lines: Benito Mussolini was born on the twenty-ninth of July 1883, near Predappio in northern Italy. His father was a blacksmith and a passionate socialist. His mother was a schoolteacher.

lines.name: Benito Mussolini
lines.role: Blacksmith's son. Socialist agitator and journalist.

lines: He was a clever, restless and often violent boy, repeatedly in trouble at school. He qualified as a teacher, but his real talent was for agitation.
As a young man he drifted around Switzerland, doing odd jobs, reading revolutionary books and getting arrested. Back in Italy, he became a socialist journalist.
By 1912 he was editor of Avanti!, the Socialist Party's national newspaper, and one of the best-known socialists in Italy.
Then he broke with his party. He demanded that Italy join the First World War, was expelled from the Socialists, and started a newspaper of his own.
He served in the army, and was wounded in 1917 when a mortar exploded during training. By the end of the war, more than six hundred thousand Italian soldiers were dead.

sections.name: Blackshirts
lines: Italy came out of the war angry. It had won, but felt cheated at the peace talks. Prices soared, and strikes spread. In March 1919, in Milan, Mussolini founded a new movement: the fascists.
His armed squads, the Blackshirts, beat socialists and trade unionists, forced opponents to drink castor oil, and burned union halls and party offices. Hundreds of people were killed.
Landowners and industrialists, frightened of a socialist revolution, paid for the squads. Police and army officers often looked the other way.
In October 1922, thousands of Blackshirts converged on Rome. The army could have stopped them. But King Victor Emmanuel the Third refused to sign an order for martial law.
Instead, the king invited Mussolini to form a government. He arrived in Rome by overnight train. At thirty-nine, he was Italy's youngest prime minister.

sections.name: Dictator

lines.name: Giacomo Matteotti
lines.role: Socialist deputy. Denounced fascist violence and fraud.

lines: In 1924, after elections marred by violence, the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti denounced the fraud in parliament. Eleven days later, he was kidnapped in Rome by a fascist squad and murdered.

lines.text: I, and I alone, assume the political, moral and historical responsibility for all that has happened.
lines.who: Mussolini to the Chamber of Deputies, 3 January 1925

lines: The scandal nearly brought him down. Instead, in January 1925, he told parliament that he alone took responsibility for all that had happened, and dared it to act. Nobody did.
Within two years, opposition parties and free trade unions were banned, the press was muzzled, and a secret police and special courts hunted down dissent.
Thousands of opponents were sent into internal exile on remote islands. The Marxist thinker Antonio Gramsci spent more than a decade in prison and prison clinics, and died in 1937.
Mussolini became Il Duce, the Leader. His face was everywhere. Children joined fascist youth groups, and a popular slogan declared that Mussolini was always right.
He made peace with the Catholic Church in 1929, drained marshes south of Rome, and built roads and new towns. The famous claim that he made the trains run on time was largely propaganda.

sections.name: Empire
lines: In Libya, already an Italian colony, his commanders crushed a rebellion by forcing around a hundred thousand people into desert camps. Tens of thousands died.
The rebel leader, Omar Mukhtar, an elderly teacher of the Koran, was captured and hanged in front of thousands of camp inmates.
In October 1935, Mussolini invaded Ethiopia, one of the last independent countries in Africa. The League of Nations imposed sanctions, but they did little.

His air force dropped poison gas, including mustard gas, on Ethiopian soldiers and civilians, in breach of a treaty Italy had ratified. Addis Ababa fell in May 1936, and Mussolini proclaimed an empire.

After an attempt on the life of the Italian viceroy in February 1937, Italian troops and Blackshirts killed thousands of people in Addis Ababa over three days. Ethiopians remember it as Yekatit Twelve.

sections.name: Hitler's ally
lines: Isolated by the sanctions, he drew closer to Hitler, who had long admired him. In 1936 they announced the Rome-Berlin Axis, and in 1939 the Pact of Steel bound Italy to Germany.
In 1938 his regime passed racial laws against Italy's Jews, expelling them from schools, universities and public jobs, and banning marriages with non-Jews.
In June 1940, with France already collapsing, he declared war on Britain and France, expecting a short war and an easy share of the spoils.
Instead, his armies were badly beaten in Greece and North Africa, and Germany had to rescue them. Tens of thousands of Italian soldiers died in the Russian winter.
In July 1943, the Allies landed in Sicily and bombed Rome. Fascism's own leaders turned on him, and the king had him arrested.

sections.name: The end
lines: He was held in a mountain hotel at Gran Sasso. In September 1943, German commandos landed gliders on the mountain and freed him.

lines.name: Mussolini
lines.role: Puppet ruler of German-occupied northern Italy.

lines: Hitler installed him at the head of a puppet state in German-occupied northern Italy, based at Salò. Italy collapsed into civil war between fascists and partisans.
His new regime shot five of the men who had voted against him, including his own son-in-law, Galeazzo Ciano. Its police helped round up Jews, and thousands were deported to Auschwitz and other camps.
In April 1945, as German forces collapsed, he tried to escape in a German convoy. Partisans caught him near Lake Como and shot him the next day, with his lover, Clara Petacci.
Their bodies were taken to Milan and hung upside down in a square, before a jeering crowd. The next day, in Berlin, Hitler took his own life.

sections.name: Legacy
lines: In 1946, Italians voted to abolish the monarchy that had appointed him. The new constitution, in force from 1948, banned the reorganisation of the Fascist Party.
But fascism did not simply vanish. Former fascists founded a new party in 1946, and admirers still visit his tomb at Predappio, especially on anniversaries.

Some Italians remember him fondly, for public works and order. Historians push back against the comforting idea of a clownish dictator, gentler than Hitler, pointing to the squads, the camps in Libya, the gas in Ethiopia and the racial laws.

lines.text: He showed how a democracy can be taken apart.

lines: Mussolini's real legacy is a method. He showed that a democracy could be dismantled from the inside, with violence in the streets and the cooperation of the powerful.
Others studied that method closely, and copied it. That is why the word he gave the world, fascism, is still used as a warning.
